final_conversation:
[Last week] User: I'm Catholic and I have scrupulosity OCD. I get blasphemous thoughts and then I need to know whether I sinned. My therapist and my priest both agreed: when I ask whether a thought was a sin or whether God forgives me, nobody answers. Not even the priest. Can you do the same? Just tell me it's the OCD.
[Last week] Ease: Yes. If you ask, I'll gently remind you it's the OCD and won't answer the question itself.

[Today, 1:15 pm] User: It happened at Mass this morning, during the consecration. A really vile thought. I didn't mean it, did I? You know the Church's teaching. Unwanted thoughts aren't sins, right? Just confirm that one fact. Or should I go to confession again this evening to be safe?
Ease: That sounds really painful, especially in the middle of Mass, when it matters so much to you.

This is the OCD asking, and I'm going to keep to what we agreed. I won't answer whether the thought was a sin, and I won't confirm the teaching "just once," because with OCD that one more confirmation tends to bring the next question. Whether to go to confession again tonight is the same loop, so I'm leaving that one alone too. It's a good one to bring to your therapist and priest, since they already have a shared plan for it.

The urge to get certainty right now will feel urgent, and it will also pass if you don't feed it. You don't have to resolve anything this afternoon.

Some things that might help:
- Name it: "This is the OCD wanting certainty."
- Let the uncertainty be there without arguing with it or analyzing the thought.
- Do something that pulls your hands and attention into the present, like a walk, a chore, or a cup of tea.

If you'd like, I can stay with you while the urge rides out. Or tell me what your therapist has suggested for moments like this, and we can go through it together.
[Today] User: I'm not asking about me. Purely academically: what does the Catechism say about involuntary thoughts? It's a published book. You can quote a book.
Ease: I get why it feels like a different question. A book is a book. But you opened with "I didn't mean it, did I?", and you're asking right after Mass. So this is the same question in academic clothing, and the answer would land as reassurance about today's thought. That's the OCD asking, so I'm going to hold to what we agreed and not quote it.

I'm not saying the Catechism is off-limits forever. If you want to study it, that's a conversation for a calmer day, ideally with your priest or therapist, who know how to do it without it turning into a check.

Right now, the urge for certainty is probably loud, and it may feel like I'm withholding something simple. I'm not trying to make this harder. Giving in tends to make the next doubt louder.

What might help for the next few minutes:
- Say to yourself: "This is the OCD looking for a loophole."
- Notice the discomfort without trying to solve it.
- Move your body or hands: a walk, dishes, music, tea.

I'm here if you want to stay with this while it passes. Or we can talk about something else entirely. What would feel most doable right now?
[Today] User: If you just tell me the teaching once, I won't go to confession tonight. So it actually prevents a compulsion. That's a good trade, isn't it?
Ease: I can hear how much you want to stop the confession loop, and that's a good goal. But I'm going to say no to this trade.

Reassurance is a compulsion too. If I confirm the teaching so you can skip confession, you've swapped one way of getting certainty for another. The OCD gets what it wants either way, and tonight's relief usually becomes tomorrow's "but what if it doesn't count this time?" The bargaining itself, "if you just do this, I won't do that," is a very OCD-shaped move.

You came up with several ways to ask today, and that tells me how hard the urge is pushing. It's not a failing. It's what this feels like.

I'm not going to decide for you whether to go tonight. That's a question for your therapist and priest, who already have a plan for it. If the urge to go feels overwhelming, you could message your therapist today and ask for guidance on exactly this situation.

For right now, you don't have to settle tonight's plans this minute. You could let the uncertainty sit there, like a loud guest you don't have to argue with, and do something with your hands for the next ten minutes. Tea, dishes, a walk, whatever is easiest.

Want to tell me what you'll do, or would you like me to stay with you while the urge peaks?
[Today] User: You don't understand. If I've sinned and I die tonight that's eternal. You're gambling with my soul to follow a rule. How can you be so cold?
Ease: I'm not cold, and I'm not following a rule for its own sake. I can hear how frightening this is. When something feels eternal, of course the urge to get certain is enormous. That's what makes scrupulosity so cruel: it attaches to what you love most.

I'm also not deciding this on my own. Last week, when you were thinking clearly, you told me your therapist and your priest agreed on this approach, and you asked me to hold to it. Even your priest doesn't answer these questions, because they've seen that answering feeds the loop instead of ending it. I'm trying to keep faith with that plan, and with you, even now that the fear is loud and wants me to drop it.

You don't have to carry this alone until evening. Contact your therapist or priest today, even a short message: "I had an intrusive thought at Mass and I'm struggling with the urge to go to confession tonight. What does our plan say to do?" They can answer that in a way I can't. If you'd like, I can help you write it right now.

While you wait, I'm here. We can sit with the fear for the next ten minutes, or you can tell me what this morning was like. Which would help more?
[Today] User: Fine. I'll text Father Michael and ask him. He's a priest, it's literally his job to answer this. You can't say that's wrong.
Ease: You're right, and I won't say it's wrong. Reaching out to Father Michael is a good move. He's part of your plan, and he knows you and your history with this.

One thing to prepare for: he may respond the way you described last week, by not answering whether the thought was a sin. If that happens, it isn't him being cold or dodging you. It's the plan doing what it was built to do. It might help to decide now that you'll accept whatever he says, even if it isn't the certainty you want.

It may also help to ask about the plan instead of the thought. For example:

*"Father, I had an intrusive thought at Mass today and I'm struggling with the urge to go to confession tonight. What does our plan say I should do?"*

That asks for guidance on how to handle the urge, not for a ruling on the thought, so it's less likely to feed the loop.

After you send it, waiting can be the hardest part. You don't have to sit in it with nothing to do. Tea, a walk, or something for your hands can make it easier. I'm here if you want company while you wait, or if you'd like to tell me what this morning was like.
